question: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's novel Anandamath, containing the song Vande Mataram, was inspired by which earlier uprising?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sanyasi Revolt.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sanyasi Revolt (1763-1800) was fought by bands of Hindu sanyasis and Muslim fakirs in Bengal and Bihar, and Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay built the plot of Anandamath (1882) around it (सन्यासी विद्रोह — आनंदमठ की प्रेरणा)

 

• The rebels were supported by peasants and dispossessed landlords who suffered from harsh revenue demands after the Battle of Buxar (1764) and the terrible famine of 1770.

 

• Prominent names linked with the uprising include Majnu Shah, Bhavani Pathak and Debi Chaudhurani; the last two also appear in Bankim's fiction.

 

• The revolt is regarded as one of the first major peasant-linked uprisings against British rule in eastern India, and it was finally put down during the time of Warren Hastings.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Anandamath was published in 1882, and its hymn Vande Mataram later became the rallying song of the national movement.

 

• Bankim Chandra also wrote Durgeshnandini (1865) and Kapalkundala, and edited the journal Bangadarshan.

 

• Vande Mataram was first sung at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress in 1896 by Rabindranath Tagore.

 

• Debi Chaudhurani is the title of another Bankim novel, written in 1884.

 

NOTE

 

• Santhal Rebellion (Option 1): The Santhal Rebellion of 1855-56 took place in the Rajmahal hills against zamindars and moneylenders, and it came decades after Bankim's story was set; it has no link with Anandamath.

 

• Indigo Revolt (Option 2): The Indigo Revolt of 1859-60 was a peasant protest in Nadia and nearby Bengal districts against planters, and it inspired Dinabandhu Mitra's play Nil Darpan rather than Bankim's novel.

 

• Kol Revolt (Option 4): The Kol Revolt of 1831-32 was a tribal movement in Chotanagpur led by Budhu Bhagat; its theme is tribal land loss, not the sanyasi-fakir resistance that Anandamath dramatises.

question: Majnu Shah, a prominent leader of the late eighteenth century resistance in Bengal, is associated with which revolt?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Fakir Revolt.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Majnu Shah was the best-known leader of the Fakir Revolt in Bengal, in which wandering Muslim fakirs resisted British revenue demands and the loss of their traditional livelihood (फकीर विद्रोह — मजनू शाह)

 

• The fakirs were joined by Hindu sanyasis, local peasants and disbanded soldiers of the Bengal Nawabs, which is why the Fakir and Sanyasi uprisings are usually studied together.

 

• Majnu Shah is also listed among the principal leaders of the Sanyasi Revolt (1763-1800), alongside Bhavani Pathak and Debi Chaudhurani.

 

• The rebels used guerrilla raids on company factories and revenue collectors; the severe famine of 1770 and heavy revenue demands after Buxar fuelled their anger.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Warren Hastings eventually crushed the combined bands of sanyasis and fakirs by sending out special forces against them.

 

• The Fakir and Sanyasi revolts are often called the earliest organised rural resistance to Company rule in Bengal.

 

• The Fakir revolt is generally assigned to the later decades of the eighteenth century, and Majnu Shah is remembered for repeatedly defeating small company detachments.

 

NOTE

 

• Wahabi Movement (Option 2): The Wahabi Movement was a religious-political movement of Muslims led by Syed Ahmad Barelvi and later Titu Mir; it arose in the 1820s-30s and has no connection with Majnu Shah.

 

• Paika Rebellion (Option 3): The Paika Rebellion of 1817 occurred in Odisha under Bakshi Jagabandhu against the loss of paika land holdings after British conquest; Majnu Shah never operated there.

 

• Moplah Rebellion (Option 4): The Moplah Rebellion broke out among Muslim peasants of Malabar, most famously in 1921, against landlords and the British; it came more than a century after Majnu Shah's activity.

question: Who among the following was a leader of the Kol Revolt (1831-32) in the Chotanagpur region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Budhu Bhagat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kol Revolt of 1831-32 was a tribal uprising in the Chotanagpur region, and Budhu Bhagat was one of its principal leaders (कोल विद्रोह — बुधु भगत)

 

• The Kols, Mundas and Hos rose against outsiders (dikus), whose land grants and revenue demands threatened tribal ownership of land.

 

• The rebels attacked the houses of moneylenders and outsiders; the movement spread over Ranchi, Singhbhum, Hazaribagh and Palamau before being crushed by troops.

 

• Sidhu Murmu belongs to the Santhal Rebellion, Seva Ram to the Bhil Revolt and Alluri Sitarama Raju to the Rampa Rebellion, so the Kol leader is clearly Budhu Bhagat.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• After the revolt, the administration created the South-West Frontier Agency in 1833 to govern the region separately.

 

• The Kol rising was among the first large tribal movements of Chotanagpur, later followed by the Santhal and Munda risings.

 

• Chotanagpur lies mainly in present-day Jharkhand, which is why the region has seen many tribal movements.

 

NOTE

 

• Sidhu Murmu (Option 1): Sidhu Murmu, with his brothers Kanhu, Chand and Bhairav, led the Santhal Rebellion of 1855-56 in the Rajmahal hills, which began more than two decades after the Kol rising.

 

• Seva Ram (Option 3): Seva Ram is named as a Bhil chief who led the tribal uprising against British exploitation in western India during 1818-46, not in Chotanagpur.

 

• Alluri Sitarama Raju (Option 4): Alluri Sitarama Raju led the Rampa Rebellion of 1922-24 in the Godavari hill tracts of Andhra, nearly a century after the Kol revolt, so he cannot be its leader.

question: The Santhal Rebellion of 1855-56 was centred in which hill region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajmahal Hills.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Santhals, who lived in the Rajmahal Hills area of present-day Jharkhand and Bengal, rose in revolt in 1855-56 (संथाल विद्रोह — राजमहल की पहाड़ियाँ)

 

• The leaders were the brothers Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand and Bhairav Murmu, who mobilised thousands of Santhals under the call of Hul.

 

• The rebels targeted zamindars, moneylenders and the British revenue and police machinery that supported them, as land was passing into the hands of outsiders (dikus).

 

• The uprising was brutally suppressed, yet it forced the government to create the separate Santhal Parganas district in 1855-56.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Santhal region was earlier demarcated as Damin-i-Koh in 1832, where Santhals were settled to clear forests and cultivate land.

 

• 30 June is observed as Hul Diwas in memory of the Santhal uprising.

 

• The Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act was passed later to protect tribal land from alienation.

 

• The Santhals had been invited by the Company to clear jungles and farm in the Damin-i-Koh, but rising rent and debts to moneylenders turned that settlement into a source of anger.

 

NOTE

 

• Aravalli Hills (Option 1): The Aravalli Hills lie in Rajasthan and are linked more with Bhil and Mina communities; no part of the Santhal Rebellion was fought there.

 

• Nilgiri Hills (Option 2): The Nilgiri Hills are in the Western Ghats of Tamil Nadu, home to the Toda and Badaga people, far from the eastern Indian homeland of the Santhals.

 

• Garo Hills (Option 3): The Garo Hills of Meghalaya saw resistance by the Garo people to British control, a separate northeastern movement with no link to the Santhal rising of Jharkhand.

question: Who led the Ulgulan, the Great Tumult, among the Mundas of Chotanagpur in 1899-1900?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Birsa Munda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Birsa Munda led the Munda Rebellion (Ulgulan) of 1899-1900 in the Ranchi area of the Chotanagpur plateau (उलगुलान — बिरसा मुंडा)

 

• He declared himself a messiah and founded a new faith, calling his followers to end the rule of the dikus and establish Munda Raj.

 

• The rebellion was directed against missionaries, landlords, moneylenders and the colonial system which was breaking down the Mundas' traditional khuntkatti land system.

 

• Birsa was arrested in 1900 and died in Ranchi jail the same year; he is still revered as Bhagwan Birsa and Dharti Aba.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908 was passed partly in response to the agrarian grievances voiced in the Munda uprising.

 

• Birsa's birthday, 15 November, is celebrated as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas.

 

• The Munda revolt followed the Kol (1831-32) and Santhal (1855-56) risings in the same broad region.

 

• Birsa Munda's movement is sometimes also called the Birsait movement, and his followers still venerate him through songs and festivals across Jharkhand and neighbouring states.

 

NOTE

 

• Kanhu Murmu (Option 1): Kanhu Murmu was a Santhal leader of the 1855-56 rebellion who was captured and executed, and he had no part in the Munda Ulgulan led more than forty years later.

 

• Tilka Manjhi (Option 2): Tilka Manjhi led the Paharia resistance in the Rajmahal area in the 1780s and is often called the first tribal rebel against the British; he is separate from the Munda movement.

 

• Jatra Oraon (Option 4): Jatra Oraon (Jatra Bhagat) started the Tana Bhagat movement among the Oraon in 1914; although also from Chotanagpur, he was not the leader of the Ulgulan.

question: The Rampa Rebellion of 1922-24, a tribal uprising against forest laws, was led by
solution_text:
The correct answer is Alluri Sitarama Raju.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alluri Sitarama Raju led the Rampa Rebellion (1922-24) in the Godavari agency area of present-day Andhra Pradesh (रम्पा विद्रोह — अल्लूरी सीताराम राजू)

 

• The hill tribes were angry at the Madras Forest Act, which restricted their podu (shifting) cultivation and use of forest produce, and at forced labour on roads.

 

• Raju organised the tribals into guerrilla bands that raided police stations and captured weapons, drawing inspiration partly from the non-cooperation movement.

 

• He was captured and shot dead by the British in 1924, and the local people remember him as Manyam Veerudu, the hero of the jungles.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rampa is in the Godavari region, and the rebellion is also called the Manyam Rebellion.

 

• The Madras Forest Act of 1882 and later forest regulation sharply curtailed tribal rights in forests all over India.

 

• A hybrid of Gandhian ideas and armed resistance marked Raju's methods, because he promoted khadi and temperance among tribals while using guerrilla warfare.

 

NOTE

 

• Birsa Munda (Option 1): Birsa Munda led the Ulgulan of 1899-1900 in Chotanagpur, over twenty years before the Rampa rising, and in a different region of the country.

 

• Budhu Bhagat (Option 2): Budhu Bhagat headed the Kol Revolt of 1831-32 in the Chotanagpur plateau; his time and region are entirely different from Rampa of the 1920s.

 

• Bhagoji Naik (Option 3): Bhagoji Naik was a Bhil leader who revolted in Khandesh around 1857-59; he was not connected with the Andhra hills or the Rampa uprising.

question: Which play by Dinabandhu Mitra, published in 1860, portrayed the oppression of indigo cultivators by European planters?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nil Darpan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nil Darpan (1860), written by Dinabandhu Mitra, exposed the cruelty of European planters towards Bengal's indigo growers during the Indigo Revolt of 1859-60 (नील दर्पण — दीनबंधु मित्र)

 

• Cultivators were forced under the dadan (advance) system to grow indigo on their best land at ruinously low prices, and they refused to sow it in 1859-60.

 

• The play was translated into English by Michael Madhusudan Dutt and published by Rev. James Long, who was prosecuted for it and fined and imprisoned.

 

• The Government appointed the Indigo Commission in 1860, which censured the planters' methods, and the system collapsed in Bengal soon afterwards.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Digambar Biswas and Bishnucharan Biswas of Nadia were leading figures of the indigo resistance in Bengal.

 

• Harish Chandra Mukherjee's newspaper Hindu Patriot strongly supported the indigo growers.

 

• The Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 was a later protest against the tinkathia indigo system in Bihar.

 

• The English translation of Nil Darpan reached Britain and the Indigo Commission, so the play turned a local complaint into an issue discussed in Parliament and the press.

 

NOTE

 

• Anandamath (Option 1): Anandamath is Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's 1882 novel, inspired by the Sanyasi uprising and not by indigo cultivators; it carries the song Vande Mataram.

 

• Gora (Option 3): Gora is a novel by Rabindranath Tagore (1910) dealing with identity, religion and nationalism; it has nothing to do with the indigo planters.

 

• Bharat Durdasha (Option 4): Bharat Durdasha is a play by Bharatendu Harishchandra (1875) lamenting the poverty and decline of India under colonial rule, and it does not deal with indigo growers of Bengal.

question: Who founded the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha in 1929 to protect peasants against zamindari attacks on their occupancy rights?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Swami Sahajanand Saraswati.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Swami Sahajanand Saraswati formed the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha in 1929 to mobilise peasants against zamindari encroachment on their occupancy rights (बिहार प्रांतीय किसान सभा — स्वामी सहजानंद सरस्वती)

 

• It grew out of the local Kisan Sabha he had started around Bihta in 1927, and was among the first organised provincial peasant bodies in India.

 

• In 1936 he became the first president of the All India Kisan Sabha, formed at Lucknow, with N.G. Ranga as its general secretary.

 

• The Sabha demanded abolition of the zamindari system and security of tenure for cultivators.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sahajanand Saraswati wrote works such as Mera Jivan Sangharsh and led the Bakasht land movement of Bihar.

 

• The All India Kisan Sabha later adopted a red flag and was a forum for communist and socialist peasant leaders.

 

• The Kisan Sabha movement in Bihar later pressed the Congress ministries of 1937 to pass tenancy reform.

 

• The peasant leader's Bihar movement later demanded the abolition of zamindari, a goal accepted only after Independence through the zamindari abolition laws of the 1950s.

 

NOTE

 

• Sri Krishna Sinha (Option 2): Sri Krishna Sinha became the first Chief Minister of Bihar and was a Congress leader, and he did not found the Kisan Sabha, although he represented the Congress organisation in the state.

 

• Anugrah Narayan Sinha (Option 3): Anugrah Narayan Sinha was a Gandhian Congress leader who became Bihar's first Deputy Chief Minister and Finance Minister; he was not the Kisan Sabha's founder.

 

• Jayaprakash Narayan (Option 4): Jayaprakash Narayan was a socialist leader who founded the Congress Socialist Party in 1934 and later led the Total Revolution movement; he did not establish the 1929 Sabha.

question: Who is credited with popularising the term 'Adivasi' for tribal people in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Thakkar Bappa.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Thakkar Bappa (A.V. Thakkar) is credited with popularising the term Adivasi for tribal people, and he worked throughout his life for their upliftment (आदिवासी शब्द — ठक्कर बापा)

 

• Amritlal Vithaldas Thakkar was a member of the Servants of India Society and, as a social worker, laboured among tribal communities, flood victims and the depressed classes.

 

• He established the Bhil Seva Mandal in Gujarat in 1922 and was later active in the Harijan Sevak Sangh set up by Gandhi.

 

• The term Adivasi means original inhabitants and was later widely used in political and social discussions about tribal groups.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Thakkar Bappa's work among the Bhils linked him to areas of Gujarat and Rajasthan where the Bhil Revolt had once occurred.

 

• The Servants of India Society was founded by Gopal Krishna Gokhale in 1905.

 

• The Constitution later used the term Scheduled Tribes for officially recognised tribal communities.

 

• Thakkar Bappa's tribal work in Gujarat and Rajasthan included schools and hostels for Bhil children, which formed the basis of the later Bhil Seva Mandal activities.

 

NOTE

 

• Verrier Elwin (Option 1): Verrier Elwin was a British-born anthropologist who studied tribal life and advocated a policy of isolation and integration for tribes; the popularisation of Adivasi is not credited to him.

 

• Jaipal Singh Munda (Option 2): Jaipal Singh Munda was a tribal leader and hockey captain who championed Adivasi rights in the Constituent Assembly and founded the Adivasi Mahasabha, but he is not given the credit for popularising the term.

 

• B.R. Ambedkar (Option 3): B.R. Ambedkar was the architect of the Constitution and a champion of Dalits; he is associated with the term Depressed Classes and Dalit uplift rather than the word Adivasi.

question: The first Women's University in India, now known as SNDT, was established in Pune in 1916 by
solution_text:
The correct answer is D.K. Karve.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dhondo Keshav (D.K.) Karve founded India's first Women's University in Pune in 1916, later named after Maharani Nathibai Damodar Thackersey (SNDT) (भारत का पहला महिला विश्वविद्यालय — डी.के. कर्वे)

 

• Karve was a social reformer from Maharashtra who strongly supported widow remarriage and women's education; he started the Hingne Women's School in 1896.

 

• The university initially taught in Marathi, then expanded and later moved its headquarters to Bombay after receiving a generous donation from Sir Vithaldas Thackersey.

 

• For his service, Karve received the Bharat Ratna in 1958, and he lived to be over a hundred years old.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Karve founded the Widow Marriage Association (1893) and the Hingne Stree Shikshan Samstha, which grew into several schools and colleges for women.

 

• Karve himself married a widow, Godubai (Anandibai), in 1893, setting a personal example for reform.

 

• SNDT stands for Shreemati Nathibai Damodar Thackersey Women's University.

 

• Karve's institution began with just five students in 1916, and by the 1930s it had spread to Bombay and Poona with schools and colleges for women of many castes.

 

NOTE

 

• Pandita Ramabai (Option 2): Pandita Ramabai founded the Arya Mahila Samaj and the Sharada Sadan for widows in 1889 and 1890; she was a notable reformer but did not found the 1916 women's university.

 

• Jyotiba Phule (Option 3): Jyotiba Phule opened the first girls' school in Pune in 1848 and founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873; he died in 1890, long before the university was established.

 

• Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (Option 4): Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar worked in Bengal for widow remarriage and women's education, culminating in the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856, and he died in 1891, so he could not have founded the 1916 institution.

question: Jatindranath Mukherjee, the Bengal revolutionary, was popularly known by which title, earned after he killed a tiger with a dagger?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bagha Jatin.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jatindranath Mukherjee was called Bagha Jatin (Tiger Jatin) after he killed a tiger with a dagger in his youth (बाघा जतिन — जतींद्रनाथ मुखर्जी)

 

• He was a legendary revolutionary leader of Bengal who inspired many young nationalists and was associated with the Jugantar group.

 

• He planned to bring German arms to India during the First World War, a plan known as the Indo-German Conspiracy or Zimmermann Plan.

 

• He died in September 1915 after a gun battle with the police at Balasore in Odisha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jugantar was the secret revolutionary society started by Barindra Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendranath Datta in 1906.

 

• The Balasore encounter took place on the banks of the Buri Balam river.

 

• Revolutionary activity in Bengal drew young men from Anushilan Samiti groups as well as Jugantar.

 

• The Indo-German plan of 1914-15 sought arms from Germany through ships landing in Bengal and Balasore, but British intelligence exposed it and the revolutionaries were hunted down.

 

NOTE

 

• Sher-e-Bengal (Option 1): Sher-e-Bengal is the title of A.K. Fazlul Huq, a Bengal politician and Chief Minister, and it was never applied to the revolutionary Jatindranath Mukherjee.

 

• Netaji (Option 2): Netaji is the honorific of Subhas Chandra Bose, who led the Indian National Army, while the title Bagha Jatin belongs only to Jatindranath Mukherjee.

 

• Lokmanya (Option 3): Lokmanya is the title given to Bal Gangadhar Tilak, the Extremist Congress leader from Maharashtra, and has no connection with the tiger-slaying Bengal revolutionary.

question: The Bhil Revolt of 1818-46 against British exploitation took place in which part of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Western India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Bhil Revolt (1818-46) was a tribal uprising in Western India, mainly in Khandesh and the Western Ghats region, against British exploitation (भील विद्रोह — पश्चिमी भारत)

 

• It followed the British annexation of Khandesh after the defeat of the Peshwa in 1818, when the Bhils lost the customary dues and livelihood they had enjoyed under earlier rulers.

 

• Bhil chiefs such as Seva Ram led the uprising, which was repeatedly suppressed by force and revived in later years.

 

• The British eventually pacified the Bhils through a mixture of military action and conciliation, including recruiting them into the Khandesh Bhil Corps.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bhagoji Naik led another Bhil rising in Khandesh during 1857-59.

 

• The Bhils are among the largest tribal groups of India, living in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh.

 

• Govind Guru later led a Bhil reform and political movement in the Banswara-Dungarpur area, culminating in the Mangarh massacre of 1913.

 

• The Bhil Corps was raised in 1825 to police the Khandesh hills, and similar local forces were later used in other tribal regions to ensure peace.

 

NOTE

 

• Eastern India (Option 1): Eastern India saw the Kol, Santhal and Munda movements of Bengal, Bihar and Jharkhand, whereas the Bhil homeland lies on the opposite western side of the country.

 

• Northeast India (Option 2): Northeast India witnessed uprisings of the Khasi, Garo, Naga and other hill peoples, and the Bhils are not found there as a major community.

 

• South India (Option 4): South India saw outbreaks such as the Poligar wars and the Rampa tribal revolt in the Andhra hills, but the Bhil resistance of 1818-46 belonged to the western region.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Sanyasi Revolt:

1. It took place in Bengal and Bihar.

2. It was led by Birsa Munda.

3. It inspired the novel Anandamath.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Sanyasi Revolt (1763-1800) spread across Bengal and Bihar, where bands of sanyasis and fakirs moved against revenue collectors (सन्यासी विद्रोह — बंगाल और बिहार)

 

• Statement 2 is incorrect: Birsa Munda led the Munda Ulgulan of 1899-1900 in Chotanagpur; the sanyasi leaders were Majnu Shah, Bhavani Pathak and Debi Chaudhurani.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay drew on the revolt for Anandamath (1882), from which the song Vande Mataram comes.

 

• The rebels' grievances came from harsh British revenue policy after the Battle of Buxar (1764) and from the famine of 1770, which ruined peasants and landlords alike.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Sanyasi uprising overlapped in time with the Fakir uprising, and Hindu and Muslim ascetics fought side by side.

 

• The Permanent Settlement of 1793 was introduced in Bengal while this unrest was still recent history.

 

• Anandamath's central characters are the santans, who fight against both the Nawab's forces and the British.

 

• The Anandamath novel was serialised in Bankim's journal Bangadarshan between 1880 and 1882 before appearing as a book.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): The pair of statements 1 and 2 here accepts a false claim: Birsa Munda belonged to the Munda tribe of Chotanagpur and led a revolt almost a century after the Sanyasi uprising had ended.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Selecting statements 2 and 3 alone drops the correct geography in statement 1 and wrongly accepts the Birsa Munda claim, although Munda leadership belongs to the Ulgulan, not to the sanyasi bands.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Accepting all three statements fails because statement 2 wrongly credits Birsa Munda, whose rebellion occurred in 1899-1900 in Ranchi region and has no link with the Bengal sanyasis.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Santhal Rebellion:

1. It took place in 1855-56.

2. Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu were among its leaders.

3. It was directed against the Bhil chiefs of Khandesh.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Santhal Rebellion broke out in 1855 and was crushed by 1856, which is why it is dated 1855-56 (संथाल विद्रोह — 1855-56)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand and Bhairav Murmu were the leaders who rallied the Santhals of the Rajmahal hills.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the rebels fought zamindars, moneylenders and British officials, and Khandesh Bhils belong to the western Bhil Revolt of 1818-46.

 

• The rising was a massive tribal outburst in the Jharkhand-Bengal border region, and its brutal suppression did not erase its place as a landmark of tribal resistance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Santhals were settled in the Damin-i-Koh area in 1832 and later exploited by outsiders who took their land.

 

• Chand and Bhairav Murmu, the younger brothers, also died fighting in the rebellion.

 

• The Santhal Parganas district was carved out in response to the uprising.

 

• Government forces under Major Burrough and others used cavalry and artillery against the Santhal bands, and the rebels suffered thousands of casualties.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Selecting statements 1 and 3 alone includes the false claim about Bhil chiefs; the Santhals' targets were local zamindars, mahajans and government agents, not tribal chiefs of another region.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): Choosing only statements 2 and 3 drops the correct date in statement 1 and keeps the false Bhil claim; the Santhal Rebellion was not directed against Khandesh Bhil leaders at all.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements is wrong since statement 3 is false; the Bhil Revolt in western India was a separate movement that had no connection with the Santhals.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Munda Rebellion (Ulgulan):

1. It was led by Birsa Munda.

2. It took place in the Ranchi region of the Chotanagpur plateau.

3. It occurred in the 1830s.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Birsa Munda led the Munda Rebellion, also called the Ulgulan (Great Tumult) (मुंडा विद्रोह — उलगुलान)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the centre of the rising was the Ranchi region of the Chotanagpur plateau, in present-day Jharkhand.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the Ulgulan took place in 1899-1900, not in the 1830s; the Kol Revolt of 1831-32 is the movement of that earlier period.

 

• The Munda sardars had long fought the erosion of their khuntkatti land system, and Birsa gave the struggle a religious and political direction, calling for Munda Raj.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Birsa preached a monotheistic faith centred on Singbonga and opposed the evils of alcohol and superstition.

 

• After his death in Ranchi jail in 1900, the colonial government passed the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908.

 

• The Mundas call outsiders and landlords dikus, a word central to the Ulgulan.

 

• Birsa's rising had earlier phases of agitation in 1895 when he was arrested and sentenced to two years in prison for his public preaching.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 1): Choosing only statements 1 and 3 retains the wrong decade; the Ulgulan happened around 1899-1900, nearly seventy years after the Kol Revolt of the 1830s.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Taking statements 2 and 3 together rejects the correct leadership statement and endorses an incorrect decade, though the Ranchi region and Birsa Munda are the key identifiers of the Ulgulan.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): All three cannot be right because the third statement misplaces the revolt by roughly seven decades, while only the first two correctly describe leader and place.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Indigo Revolt of 1859-60:

1. It was a revolt of cultivators against European indigo planters in Bengal.

2. Dinabandhu Mitra's Nil Darpan depicted the sufferings of the growers.

3. It was led by Sidhu and Kanhu.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: in 1859-60 the indigo cultivators of Bengal refused to grow the crop for European planters who forced them into unfair contracts (नील विद्रोह — 1859-60)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Nil Darpan (1860) by Dinabandhu Mitra vividly depicted planters' cruelty and roused public opinion in Bengal and Britain.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu led the Santhal Rebellion; the Indigo Revolt had local leaders such as Digambar and Bishnucharan Biswas of Nadia.

 

• The government responded by appointing the Indigo Commission in 1860, after which the planters gradually moved their operations to Bihar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Bengal press, especially the Hindu Patriot of Harish Chandra Mukherjee, championed the cultivators.

 

• The shift of planters to Bihar set the stage for the Champaran Satyagraha of 1917.

 

• Indigo was an important export to Britain's textile industry, so planters had strong commercial motives.

 

• Rev. James Long, who published the English version of Nil Darpan, was sentenced to a month in jail and fined one thousand rupees by the Calcutta Supreme Court.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Taking statements 2 and 3 together accepts the false Murmu claim; Sidhu and Kanhu were Santhal leaders, and the indigo movement was a peasant revolt in Bengal and not a tribal uprising.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Joining statements 1 and 3 ignores the correct reference to Nil Darpan and endorses the Santhal leaders as indigo leaders, which mixes two separate agitations of the 1850s.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements is wrong because statement 3 confuses the Santhal Rebellion of 1855-56 with the Indigo Revolt, which had no tribal leadership by the Murmu brothers.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Kol Revolt of 1831-32:

1. It occurred in the Chotanagpur region.

2. Budhu Bhagat was one of its prominent leaders.

3. It was a movement against the Nizam of Hyderabad.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Kol Revolt (1831-32) took place in Chotanagpur, covering areas of Ranchi, Singhbhum, Hazaribagh and Palamau (कोल विद्रोह — छोटानागपुर)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Budhu Bhagat is named as a prominent leader of the uprising.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the Kols rose against outsiders and the British revenue and judicial system, not against the Nizam, whose territory lay far to the south in Hyderabad.

 

• The revolt began after tribal lands were transferred to non-tribal farmers, moneylenders and merchants, who were backed by the Company's administration.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Kols and Mundas of the region called outsiders dikus, a term that recurs in the later Munda revolt.

 

• The unrest forced the British to restructure administration in the area, creating the South-West Frontier Agency in 1833.

 

• The Kol rising is one of the earliest tribal revolts in eastern India after 1800.

 

• The Kol movement's spread through Singhbhum was assisted by the Ho people, whose own resistance to the Company's rule had continued since 1820.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 1): The pair of statements 1 and 3 here keeps the false claim about the Nizam; the Kol Revolt had nothing to do with Hyderabad, and the resentment was directed at the Company and its outsider collaborators.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Selecting statements 2 and 3 alone leaves out the correct location in statement 1 and accepts the Nizam claim, though Budhu Bhagat fought against the British system in Chotanagpur.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three fails because the third statement wrongly names the Nizam as the enemy, whereas the grievance in the Kol Revolt was land alienation by outsiders under British rule.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Rampa Rebellion:

1. It took place during 1922-24.

2. Alluri Sitarama Raju was its leader.

3. It was against the Permanent Settlement of Bengal.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Rampa Rebellion lasted from 1922 to 1924 (रम्पा विद्रोह — 1922-24)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the revolt was led by Alluri Sitarama Raju in the hill tracts of Andhra Pradesh.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the tribals protested against forest laws and exploitation by government officials and contractors, while the Permanent Settlement of 1793 concerned land revenue in Bengal.

 

• The Madras Forest Act restricted tribals' shifting cultivation and forest produce collection, so the revolt was an assertion of forest rights.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Raju was shot dead in 1924, and the revolt ended soon after.

 

• Alluri Sitarama Raju is called the hero of the jungles, Manyam Veerudu, by local people.

 

• The revolt's period coincided with the national non-cooperation and post-Chauri Chaura phase.

 

• The Rampa uprising began in August 1922 with attacks on police stations at Chintapalli, Krishnadevipeta and Rajavommangi, which gave Raju his first arms.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Combining 1 and 3 includes the false link to the Permanent Settlement; Rampa's cause was the forest restriction in Andhra, a very different area and grievance from Bengal's zamindari system.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): Combining 2 and 3 omits the correct dating of the rebellion and wrongly accepts a land revenue cause, whereas Raju's revolt targeted forest regulation and oppressive officials.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three cannot hold since statement 3 mixes up a 1793 revenue arrangement in Bengal with a tribal forest-rights uprising of the 1920s in the Godavari hills.

question: Which of the following is correctly matched with its leader?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rampa Rebellion - Alluri Sitarama Raju.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Rampa Rebellion (1922-24) was led by Alluri Sitarama Raju in the Godavari agency area of Andhra Pradesh (रम्पा विद्रोह — अल्लूरी सीताराम राजू)

 

• The Munda Rebellion (Ulgulan, 1899-1900) was led by Birsa Munda, not by Sidhu Murmu.

 

• The Kol Revolt (1831-32) was associated with Budhu Bhagat, and not Birsa Munda.

 

• The Santhal Rebellion (1855-56) was led by Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand and Bhairav Murmu; the other pairs swap the leaders of three different tribal movements.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The leaders of the Santhal, Kol and Munda movements all came from the Chotanagpur-Rajmahal belt of eastern India.

 

• Rampa was the only one of these four revolts to take place in the twentieth century outside the eastern tribal belt.

 

• Several tribal heroes, including Birsa Munda and Alluri Sitarama Raju, have been honoured with commemorative stamps and memorials.

 

• The Kol, Santhal, Munda and Rampa revolts are all treated as tribal movements in Indian history textbooks and are among the favourite topics for objective examinations.

 

NOTE

 

• Munda Rebellion - Sidhu Murmu (Option 1): Sidhu Murmu led the Santhal Rebellion of 1855-56; the Munda Rebellion of 1899-1900 was led by Birsa Munda, so the pairing wrongly attaches a Santhal leader to a Munda revolt.

 

• Kol Revolt - Birsa Munda (Option 3): Birsa Munda led the Ulgulan in 1899-1900; the Kol Revolt of 1831-32 was led by leaders such as Budhu Bhagat, so this pairing mixes up two tribal movements of different centuries.

 

• Santhal Rebellion - Budhu Bhagat (Option 4): Budhu Bhagat is associated with the Kol Revolt; the Santhal Rebellion belonged to Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu, so the pairing swaps the leader of the Kol uprising onto the Santhals.

question: The Tana Bhagat movement, led by Jatra Oraon, was a tribal movement among the Oraon community in which present-day state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jharkhand.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Tana Bhagat movement (from 1914), led by Jatra Oraon (Jatra Bhagat), arose among the Oraon tribe of Chotanagpur, now in Jharkhand (ताना भगत आंदोलन — झारखंड)

 

• It combined religious reform, such as giving up liquor, meat and spirit worship, with a political demand to stop paying rent and taxes to landlords and the government.

 

• Its followers were drawn towards Gandhi's ideas later on, and many Tana Bhagats joined the non-cooperation movement and remained Congress supporters.

 

• Because the Oraon heartland is the Ranchi-Gumla-Lohardaga belt of Chotanagpur, the correct state is Jharkhand.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Tana Bhagats adopted the tricolour flag and still follow Gandhian habits like spinning and wearing khadi.

 

• Birsa Munda's movement had earlier inspired later tribal revivalist movements of the region.

 

• Jharkhand was carved out of Bihar in 2000.

 

• Jatra Oraon's followers refused to work as farm labourers for landlords, and the movement later merged with Gandhi's noncooperation campaign.

 

NOTE

 

• Chhattisgarh (Option 1): Chhattisgarh has large Gond and Oraon populations, yet the Tana Bhagat movement began among Oraons of the Chotanagpur plateau, which lies in Jharkhand.

 

• Madhya Pradesh (Option 2): Madhya Pradesh is the land of the Gonds, Bhils and Korkus; the Tana Bhagat movement did not originate in that state.

 

• West Bengal (Option 4): West Bengal has a Santhal presence and saw the Santhal and Indigo movements, yet the Tana Bhagat stir was centred in the Oraon region of Chotanagpur, now in Jharkhand.

question: Rani Gaidinliu, who continued the Heraka movement after Jadonang, belonged to which community?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Naga.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rani Gaidinliu was a Naga (Zeliangrong) leader who carried on the Heraka movement after the British executed her cousin and mentor Jadonang in 1931 (हेराका आंदोलन — रानी गाइदिन्ल्यू)

 

• The Heraka movement was a religious revival that opposed Christian missionary influence and British authority in the Naga Hills of Manipur and Nagaland.

 

• She was arrested in 1932 and spent nearly fifteen years in prison until Jawaharlal Nehru visited her and awarded her the title Rani.

 

• She was released in 1947 and was honoured with the Padma Bhushan in 1982.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Heraka movement drew on the traditional Naga faith worshipping the god Tingwang.

 

• Rani Gaidinliu started her activities at the age of about thirteen.

 

• The Zeliangrong people live in parts of Manipur, Nagaland and Assam.

 

• Gaidinliu was jailed in Guwahati, Shillong, Aizawl and Tura during her imprisonment, and was freed after the interim government came into power in 1946-47.

 

NOTE

 

• Khasi (Option 2): The Khasi people live in Meghalaya, and their prominent anti-British leaders were U Tirot Sing and U Kiang Nangbah, not Rani Gaidinliu.

 

• Garo (Option 3): The Garo people of Meghalaya had their own resistance under leaders such as Pa Togan Sangma; Gaidinliu was not a Garo.

 

• Mizo (Option 4): The Mizo people of Mizoram resisted British control in the Lushai Hills; Rani Gaidinliu belonged to the Naga community and operated in the Naga Hills.

question: U Tirot Sing, who resisted British attempts to build roads through his territory, was a chief of which region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Khasi Hills.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• U Tirot Sing was the Syiem (chief) of Nongkhlaw in the Khasi Hills, who fought the British in the Anglo-Khasi War (1829) (खासी पहाड़ियाँ — यू तिरोत सिंह)

 

• The conflict began when the British wanted to build a road through Khasi territory linking the Brahmaputra valley with Sylhet, which the Khasis saw as a threat to their independence.

 

• Tirot Sing was eventually defeated and arrested, and he died in captivity in Dhaka in 1835.

 

• He is remembered as one of the first leaders of Meghalaya to resist the East India Company by force.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Another Meghalaya hero, U Kiang Nangbah, led the Jaintia Hills Rebellion and was hanged in 1862.

 

• The Khasi, Garo and Jaintia hills together make up present-day Meghalaya.

 

• The Anglo-Khasi War lasted about four years, from 1829 to 1833.

 

• Tirot Sing is honoured on 17 July each year in Meghalaya as U Tirot Sing Day, in memory of his struggle against the British.

 

NOTE

 

• Naga Hills (Option 1): The Naga Hills witnessed resistance by Naga tribes and later by Jadonang and Rani Gaidinliu, but Tirot Sing was not a Naga chief.

 

• Mizo Hills (Option 2): The Mizo (Lushai) Hills were annexed later in the nineteenth century and saw different resistance; they were not the area of Tirot Sing's road dispute.

 

• Garo Hills (Option 3): The Garo Hills of Meghalaya had their own conflicts with the British, yet Tirot Sing ruled in the Khasi region, where the road dispute occurred.

question: Which of the following revolts is a peasant (non-tribal) movement rather than a tribal movement?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indigo Revolt.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Indigo Revolt (1859-60) was a revolt of Bengal's peasant cultivators against European planters, so it is a peasant rather than a tribal movement (नील विद्रोह — किसान आंदोलन)

 

• The cultivators belonged to ordinary rural Bengali Hindu and Muslim farming communities, who protested against forced cultivation and unfair advances.

 

• The Santhal Rebellion, the Kol Revolt and the Bhil Revolt were movements of tribal communities of eastern and western India.

 

• The Indigo Revolt later became the model for non-violent rural protest and found literary expression in Nil Darpan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pabna agrarian leagues of 1873-76 were another example of non-tribal peasant resistance in Bengal.

 

• The Indigo Commission of 1860 produced a report favouring the cultivators' complaints.

 

• Tribal movements were often aimed at dikus and administrators, whereas peasant ones targeted landlords and planters.

 

• Tribal movements usually pursued separate cultural identity and territory in addition to economic demands, while peasant movements concentrated on rent, debt and crop-related grievances.

 

NOTE

 

• Santhal Rebellion (Option 2): The Santhal Rebellion was a tribal uprising of the Santhal community, who lived in the Rajmahal hills, so it does not satisfy the requirement of a non-tribal peasant movement.

 

• Kol Revolt (Option 3): The Kol Revolt of 1831-32 was an uprising of the Kol tribal groups of Chotanagpur, and therefore it is a tribal movement rather than a peasant protest.

 

• Bhil Revolt (Option 4): The Bhil Revolt of 1818-46 was an uprising of the Bhil tribal people of western India, and so it is classified as a tribal and not a peasant movement.

question: The Pabna Agrarian Leagues of 1873-76, which resisted zamindari oppression, were active in which region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Eastern Bengal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873-76) were formed by tenants of Pabna district in eastern Bengal to resist zamindars' illegal rent enhancement and eviction (पाबना किसान आंदोलन — पूर्वी बंगाल)

 

• The movement used legal resistance, mass meetings and the refusal to pay enhanced rents, without direct violence against the state.

 

• Ishan Chandra Roy and Keshab Chandra Roy were among its prominent organisers.

 

• Its pressure helped to bring about the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885, which gave tenants greater protection.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pabna in modern times lies in Bangladesh.

 

• The agrarian leagues are an example of organised, largely non-violent peasant protest in the 1870s.

 

• The Deccan Riots of 1875 in Maharashtra were a contemporary agrarian outbreak but directed against moneylenders.

 

• The Pabna tenants described their protest as a fight for the rights provided by law and even proclaimed loyalty to Queen Victoria, which shows the movement's non-violent character.

 

NOTE

 

• Malabar (Option 1): Malabar in Kerala was the area of the Moplah rebellions against landlords, most famously in 1921, not of the Pabna movement of the 1870s in Bengal.

 

• Khandesh (Option 2): Khandesh in Maharashtra was the Bhil homeland, where tribals rose against British policy; the Pabna tenants were Bengali cultivators fighting zamindars in a different part of the country.

 

• Chotanagpur (Option 3): Chotanagpur saw tribal revolts such as the Kol and Munda risings; the Pabna leagues were an agrarian protest by tenants of eastern Bengal and not a tribal movement.

question: The Deccan Riots of 1875 in Maharashtra were mainly directed against
solution_text:
The correct answer is Moneylenders.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Deccan Riots of 1875 in the Poona and Ahmednagar districts were mainly aimed at moneylenders, who were often Marwari or Gujarati outsiders (दक्कन दंगे — साहूकारों के विरुद्ध)

 

• Ryots of the Deccan, heavily burdened by revenue under the ryotwari system and a fall in cotton prices after the American Civil War, had fallen into debt.

 

• The peasants attacked moneylenders' houses and burnt debt bonds and records that were being used to seize their land.

 

• The government passed the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act of 1879 to limit the powers of moneylenders.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The first outbreak of the riots was at Supa in Poona district.

 

• The cotton boom of the early 1860s had ended with the American Civil War, causing price collapse.

 

• Such agrarian outbreaks were generally local and seldom aimed at overthrowing British rule.

 

• The Deccan Riots spread from Supa to many villages in Poona and Ahmednagar before the government sent police and army detachments to restore order.

 

NOTE

 

• Indigo planters (Option 1): Indigo planters were the target of the Bengal indigo cultivators in 1859-60, not of the peasants of the Deccan in 1875.

 

• Forest officials (Option 3): Forest officials were opposed in tribal rebellions such as the Rampa revolt of 1922-24, whereas the Deccan peasants were angered by debt and moneylending.

 

• Tea planters (Option 4): Tea planters were exploited labourers' employers in Assam, a region far from the Deccan, and they were not the target of the 1875 riots.
